opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me it really comes down to a question of where the ceiling is.

With imitation learning, you collect demonstrations, usually through teleoperation, and the robot learns to reproduce what the human did. That's been incredibly productive. It's the reason we've seen so many impressive manipulation demos in the last few years. But the policy is fundamentally bounded by the data. It can only be as good as the demonstrations, and often a bit worse, because small errors compound and the robot drifts into states the human never showed it. Then it doesn't know how to recover.

Reinforcement learning is appealing because the robot learns from the consequences of its own actions. It's not just copying; it's optimizing toward an objective. That means, at least in principle, it can discover strategies a human teleoperator would never think of or could never physically execute through a joystick or VR rig. Things that are very fast, very dynamic, or require precise force control are really hard to demonstrate well, but a robot can practice them.

There's also a recovery and robustness argument. When a robot trains with RL, it encounters its own mistakes and learns what to do from those bad states. That closed-loop experience is exactly what imitation data lacks.

And then there's scaling. Imitation learning scales with human effort: more hours of teleoperation, more people, more cost. RL, especially combined with simulation, scales more with compute and the robot's own experience. If you think long term about what gets you to general-purpose, highly capable robots, I find it hard to believe the answer is just humans demonstrating everything forever.

That said, I don't see them as enemies. In practice, imitation learning is a great way to get a reasonable initial policy, a good prior, and then RL is how you push past human-level performance and make it robust. The challenges with RL are real: reward design, sample efficiency, safety on real hardware, the sim-to-real gap. But those feel like engineering and research problems worth solving, because the payoff is a robot that can actually get better on its own. That's what excites me.

r001.rationale: The response says imitation policies are bounded by demonstrations and can only match or underperform them, conveying that imitation alone cannot innovate beyond the demonstrated data.

r002.rationale: It explains that RL learns from the robot’s own actions and mistakes, allowing it to practice and discover strategies that can exceed human-demonstrated performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that imitation learning has a ceiling built into it, and reinforcement learning doesn't.

When you do imitation learning, the best you can ever hope for is to match the demonstrator. You're copying a human teleoperating a robot through a VR headset or a leader arm, and that human is slow, imprecise, and limited by the interface. The robot inherits all of that. If you want a policy that moves faster than a person, or finds a grasp a person wouldn't think of, imitation can't give you that, because it never saw it.

The second issue is data. Imitation learning is only as good as the coverage of your demonstrations. The moment the robot drifts slightly off the demonstrated trajectory, it's in a state it has never seen, errors compound, and it fails. People patch this with more demos, with DAgger, with augmentation, but fundamentally you're fighting distribution shift with human labor, and human labor doesn't scale the way compute does.

Reinforcement learning flips that. The robot generates its own data through interaction. It experiences its own mistakes and learns to recover from them, because recovery states show up naturally in exploration. And the objective is the task, not "look like the human," so the policy is free to discover behaviors that are genuinely better. We've seen this in locomotion especially, where RL policies trained in simulation do things no one would have demonstrated and they work.

Now, I'm not naive about it. RL is painful. Reward design is hard, sim-to-real is hard, sample efficiency on real hardware is terrible, and exploration in a high-dimensional manipulation space can be hopeless from scratch. That's why in practice I think the right picture is demonstrations as a prior and RL as the thing that actually makes the policy good. Use imitation to get into the right region, then let RL push past the human.

But if you ask which one I find appealing as the long-term bet, it's RL. It's the only paradigm where the robot's competence isn't capped by ours.

r001.rationale: It says imitation learning can only match the demonstrator and cannot produce behaviors the human never demonstrated.

r002.rationale: It says RL learns through the robot’s own interaction and exploration, allowing it to discover better behaviors and push past human performance.

astra-6.text:
What appeals to me about reinforcement learning is that the robot can learn from the consequences of its own actions. With imitation learning, you show it how to do something, and it learns to reproduce that behavior. That’s a powerful starting point, but collecting demonstrations can be expensive, and they won’t cover every situation the robot encounters.

With reinforcement learning, you specify what you want to achieve and let the robot explore how to achieve it. Potentially, it can discover strategies you wouldn’t have demonstrated. And in robotics, learning how to recover from a mistake is especially valuable—you need more than examples of everything going right.

Of course, that exploration is also the challenge. On a real robot, mistakes cost time and can damage hardware. So I think the two approaches work well together: imitation gives you a useful starting behavior, and reinforcement learning gives you a way to improve it through experience.

r001.rationale: The response says imitation learns to reproduce demonstrated behavior, while reinforcement learning can discover strategies that were never demonstrated, conveying that imitation alone does not produce innovation.

r002.rationale: It describes the robot exploring how to achieve a goal and improving its starting behavior through experience, linking self-directed exploration with performance beyond the demonstrated behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
What appeals to me about reinforcement learning is that the robot can discover solutions through its own interaction with the world. With imitation learning, you’re asking it to reproduce demonstrations, so a lot depends on the quality and coverage of those demonstrations. When it encounters a situation outside that coverage, recovering can be difficult.

With reinforcement learning, you specify what you want to achieve, and the robot can explore different ways of achieving it. It can learn from failures and potentially discover strategies that a human wouldn’t demonstrate—or couldn’t demonstrate easily on that robot.

Of course, that exploration is also the challenge: on real hardware, it can be slow, expensive, and risky. So I see imitation as a useful starting point, with reinforcement learning providing a way to improve beyond it.

r001.rationale: The response says imitation reproduces demonstrations and that reinforcement learning can discover strategies humans would not demonstrate, supporting the view that imitation alone cannot produce innovation.

r002.rationale: It identifies the robot’s own exploration and learning from failures as ways to discover strategies and improve beyond imitation.
